headline.main: "Let Us Die Together": A Reporter in Gaza Who Lost His Family
headline.social: "Let Us Die Together": A Reporter in Gaza Who Lost His Family

intro: Reporter Wael Al-Dahdouh lost half of his family in the war in Gaza. The entire world was watching as he embraced the dead body of his grandchild. His reaction to the loss brought him fame throughout the Arab world.
text:
TV reporter Wael al-Dahdouh is standing on the roof of a building in Gaza City filing a report for broadcaster Al Jazeera. Sirens are wailing as he says: "It could be a bloody night.” It’s October 25, 2023. The moderator back in the studio in Doha asks Dahdouh, the station’s bureau chief in Gaza, for his thoughts on Israel’s strategy.
Dahdouh, though, says nothing. Ten seconds go by. Voices can be heard in the background. "Wael? Wael?” the moderator says. "I don’t know if you can hear me. We’re live.” Then, the voice of the producer can be heard: "The girl is in the hospital.” The moderator switches back to the studio.
Wael al-Dahdouh, already a well-known reporter in Arab countries by this point, was right. The night of October 25 was a bloody one.
For his own family.
His wife Amna, his son Mahmoud, 16, his daughter Sham, 7, his grandson Adam, 18 months, all died in an Israeli strike on a residential building in Nuseirat.
Later, the world was watching as Dahdouh, 54 years old, arrived at Al-Aqsa Hospital and embraced the lifeless body of his grandchild. Countless people holding cameras and smartphones can be seen gathered around him, filming as Dahdouh hands the small body to the doctors and stumbles further to the lifeless body of his son Mahmoud, as his tears run across the blood-smeared face of his teenage son, as he caresses him, gasps and says more to himself than to those surrounding him: "They are taking revenge on our children. Ma’alesh, no worries. We came from God and to God we shall return.”
"The Mountain" of Gaza
A short time later, now standing in a hospital hallway, Dahdouh says into a camera: "So that is the safe humanitarian zone that the Israeli occupation is talking about.” With a bitter laugh, he adds: "The moral army!”
Still wearing his press vest, he recites the prayer for the dead and tries to comfort his four surviving daughters, who are clinging to him. The cameras are still rolling.
It’s not the loss of his family that made Wael al-Dahdouh into an icon of the Arab world in the days and weeks that followed. It was his reaction to the tragedy.
The very next day, Dahdouh is again standing on the roof of the Al Jazeera bureau wearing a press vest and helmet, hands on his hips. Israeli drones are buzzing in the background as columns of smoke rise into the sky. He expresses gratitude for the solidarity and prayers he has received, and then says: "I see it as my duty to once again step in front of the cameras, despite the pain and despite the bloody wound.” He doesn’t yet know that there is plenty more pain in store for him.
Wael al-Dahdouh’s message to his people is clear: We won’t be brought down. We will continue documenting this war.
DER SPIEGEL has visited the journalist on two occasions: once in Berlin, where he received medical treatment, and once in the Qatari capital of Doha. He doesn’t seek out opportunities to tell his story and was initially opposed to an interview. And it quickly becomes clear why that is so. When speaking about the loss of his family, he avoids eye contact, fiddles with his shirt and switches from the Palestinian dialect to modern standard Arabic, as though he were reciting the news in front of a television camera.
Since the beginning of the war, triggered by the October 7 massacre in Israel perpetrated by Hamas, the Israeli military has not allowed foreign journalists to enter the Gaza Strip on their own. Even now, after the ceasefire went into effect on January 19, foreign reporters are not allowed in. A petition filed by the Foreign Press Association in Israel to gain access was denied by the highest court in Jerusalem, citing security concerns.
As a result, all the news coming from the warzone is delivered by Palestinians filming the war with their cellphones and by local journalists. Those journalists are both reporters and victims, and none of them represents this dual role to the degree Dahdouh does. Tirelessly, he marched together with tens of thousands of Palestinians as they had to leave their homes in the north on foot. Before long, Wael al-Dahdouh became "al-Jabal,” the "mountain” of Gaza. He is so patient, wrote one Arab editorialist, that even patience itself is exhausted by him.
The Israeli military, by contrast, doesn’t see journalists like al-Dahdouh as worthy of protection, but as hostile actors. It has accused numerous journalists of having close ties to Hamas, citing information that cannot be independently verified. The Israeli government sees Al Jazeera as the "mouthpiece of Hamas” and banned the broadcaster last May.
Al Jazeera is funded by the Qatari state and, according to the broadcaster’s own statistics, is available in more than 150 countries and 430 million households. Following its founding in 1996, the broadcaster also earned respect in the West because it introduced Anglo-Saxon-style journalism to the Arab world. The station achieved popularity in Arab countries primarily because of its blanket coverage of the 2011 democracy movements in several countries. In the ensuing years, however, Al Jazeera became an object of criticism because of its dependence on the Qatari government and its alleged ties to the Islamist Muslim Brotherhood and to Hamas. At the same time, though, the broadcaster continues to engage in investigative journalism even today.
Wael al-Dahdouh has been living in Doha since January 2024. The route to his home in the Qatari capital leads past the golden domes of the Galeries Lafayette department store, motorcyclists delivering food and an old World Cup poster from 2022. The guard at his gated community waves you through only after you have given the correct address.
A framed drawing stands in his extremely orderly, extremely beige living room. It depicts a child with its arms wrapped around Wael al-Dahdouh’s neck. He is smiling. In a speech bubble above the scene is the word "Ma’alesh” – "no worries.” It is a gift from a Palestinian in Qatar, a tired Dahdouh says after coming downstairs. He is wearing a splint on his right forearm, and each of his fingers is braced separately. It looks almost as though he is carrying a metal sun. His arm was badly injured in an Israeli drone strike in December 2023 as he was reporting on an Israeli attack on the Khan Younis refugee camp.
He takes a sip from his mocha as he talks about his difficulties sleeping. This morning, he says, he only fell asleep at 5:30 a.m., but he refuses to take sleeping pills. "I don’t want to become addicted to anything,” he says.
There is also a portrait of Hamza, his oldest son, in his Doha living room. Hamza was also a journalist for Al Jazeera, and on January 7, 2024, he was reporting together with colleagues from the outskirts of Rafah, the city on the southern border of the Gaza Strip. On the drive back, the Israeli military killed the 27-year-old with a drone. The army said it had identified "a terrorist” in the car who was controlling a flying object that posed "a threat” to Israeli soldiers. Reporting by DER SPIEGEL and the Washington Post indicates, however, that by the time the army targeted the car, the drone had already been on the ground for 15 minutes. And when it was in the air, it clearly hadn’t been filming Israeli positions. In cooperation with the reporting collective Forbidden Stories, DER SPIEGEL and 11 other media outlets, including the Guardian, the Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism (ARIJ) and the Israeli magazine +972, produced "The Gaza Project ,” an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the unusually high number of journalists killed in the war.
Once again, the world was watching as Wael al-Dahdouh bid farewell to a family member at the hospital. Once again, his daughters clutched him in their arms. One of them said: "Baba, we have no one left but you.” Wael al-Dahdouh left Gaza. With five instead of eight children – his daughters Bissan, Sundus, Khuloud, Batoul and his son Yehia.
A few days later, the Israeli military released a pixeled document from 2022 intended to prove that Hamza al-Dahdouh had worked for the terrorist group Islamic Jihad. The organization Reporters Without Borders was critical of the fact that Israel refused to release the document that allegedly incriminated Dahdouh. The family rejects the accusations.
Dahdouh’s case also received attention from leading politicians. During a January 7, 2024, visit to Qatar, then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken said that he was "deeply, deeply sorry for the almost unimaginable loss. I am a parent myself. I can’t begin to imagine the horror he has experienced, not once, but now twice.” It was, Blinken said, "an unimaginable tragedy.”
How does Wael al-Dahdouh manage to keep going after all the loss he has experienced? He doesn’t think long before answering with just a single word: "Rida.” It is an Islamic principle about accepting the hardest blows of fate with sanguinity, trusting that divine providence is behind them.
"The West may not be familiar with my Islam, but it helps me to remain patient and not go crazy from all the pain. An Islam free of fanaticism, an Islam of hope. We are people. We love to laugh, we love life, our children. When my child had a fever in the night, worry would keep me awake. We celebrated the wedding of my son Hamza, may God have mercy on him, for many days.”
No Prior Knowledge
There are videos of that night, showing Wael al-Dahdouh being thrown into the air by the guests. He dances with his mother, the background festooned with palms, garlands and strings of lights. It is a scene that went viral on the Arab internet, spliced together with images of the crying father at his son’s deathbed.
No other 21st century war has seen as many journalists killed as this war in Gaza. According to Reporters Without Borders, more than 150 of them have lost their lives. International law considers journalists to be civilians, as long as they don’t take part in any military operations. For that reason, the organization has filed several complaints with the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Hague.
Shortly after October 7, the pro-Israeli platform Honest Reporting ran a story that raised the question as to whether Palestinian photojournalists who were at the Israeli border that day had known about the Hamas terrorist attack beforehand. Reuters and AP immediately issued statements that they had had no prior knowledge of the attacks.
At the same time, an old selfie, shot many years before, began making the rounds. It showed Yahya Sinwar, the late Hamas leader, kissing the cheek of AP photographer Hassan Eslaiah. In response, AP and CNN severed all professional ties to Eslaiah.
Since then, though, many in the West have wondered: How close are Palestinian journalists to Hamas?
There are also photos of Wael al-Dahdouh with Yahya Sinwar. In one of them, he is giving Sinwar his hand in a staircase. When asked about the accusations leveled against him and other Palestinian journalists, Wael al-Dahdouh talks himself into a rage. "Our job as journalists is to speak with everybody. I don’t work in a vacuum. I work in Gaza. And Hamas is in charge there. Of course I’ve met with Sinwar, just like all journalists, including foreign ones. That is part of our job. The goal of these campaigns is clear: To justify our deaths.”
In a statement, Al Jazeera blamed Israel for the attack on the journalists and their families. An Israeli military spokesman told CNN in late October 2023 that they had been carrying out an attack on Hamas infrastructure in the area where members of the Dahdouh family were killed. They provided no evidence to back up the claim. The Berlin-based NGO Mnemonic has taken a closer look at the October 25, 2023, incident. DER SPIEGEL has obtained a copy of the 78-page report.
Dreams of Becoming a Doctor
The organization sees itself as a "digital memory in times of war,” with the 47 staff members focused on reconstructing war operations from a distance. To do so, they examine publicly available information and archive it. Hadi al-Khatib of Syria founded Mnemonic in 2018. "There is no evidence,” he told DER SPIEGEL, "to indicate the presence of Hamas fighters or structures in the residential complex where a German-Palestinian family and the family of Wael al-Dahdouh was killed.”
In a life free of Israeli occupation, Wael al-Dahdouh says in Doha as his grandchildren race through the room, he would have become a doctor. But instead of traveling to Iraq at age 17 with a grant to study medicine, he, the son of farmers, ended up in an Israeli prison. The First Intifada, the Palestinian uprising against the Israeli occupation, broke out in late 1987. Like many other Palestinians among his Gaza acquaintances, Wael al-Dahdouh joined demonstrations and, he says, was arrested a few months later. He spent seven years behind bars before then studying journalism in Gaza upon his release. He says he was tortured but declines to provide details. "In a phase of life when a boy becomes a man, I was all alone. I was a child who just wanted to survive in prison.”
Dahdouh’s 13-year-old son Yehia, sitting next to him, says in a firm voice: "Baba, I’m the most similar to you of all your children, right?” His father smiles and ruffles the boy’s black hair, which has grown back in after he sustained a serious head injury on the night of October 25, 2023.
Wael al-Dahdouh says he frequently finds himself thinking back to that last telephone call a couple of days before the attack. His wife Amna, who only called him at work when the family was once again running out of food because of the war, was in tears: "Wael, come home. Let us die together.” But Wael al-Dahdouh couldn’t go home that evening. It was far too dangerous to move through the city, especially after dark.
When Wael al-Dahdouh speaks about his wife, an impish grin spreads across his face, with laugh lines around his dark eyes. He remembers how he first told Amna about his feelings for her as a young man. Her older brother, he says, was opposed to the liaison, but Wael fought for her. "It was my best decision,” he says.
Sometimes, says al-Dahdouh, he tries to think of the nice days, of the holidays when he left his press vest in the closet and instead put on the Thaub, a long cotton robe. He would go to Friday prayers with his children, visit his parents and only eat half as much as he wanted to so as not to upset his wife. They would spend the rest of the day together in the garden.
"We had a palace right in the middle of a warzone. My garden had roses of all colors. I planted the best mango varieties. I am convinced that a divine relationship develops between the gardener and his plants. When you play music or recordings of the Koran for them, the plants flourish even more splendidly. But none of that remains. It was all destroyed by Israeli bombs.”
Wael al-Dahdouh points to the barren balcony across the way. "It badly needs to be greener here,” he says. "I need to be surrounded by beauty.”
Chirping can be heard from upstairs. It comes from a small, white bird his son-in-law is carrying down in a cage. "When Wael was still in Germany, the bird was quiet most of the time. Now, he doesn’t stop chirping,” he says with a grin.
Wael al-Dahdouh spent four months receiving treatment in Berlin. He says he found it difficult to speak openly in a country that so clearly took one side in this war. Germany, he says, is blind in one eye and deaf in one ear. "This war has confirmed painful truths: Many people here aren’t interested the suffering of our people. Where is the outcry from journalists? From my colleagues? The indifference of so many people kills us Palestinians just like Israel’s missiles.”
And yet, he still wanted to speak with a German media outlet. "I am a living witness,” he says. "If people don’t listen to me, who will they listen to?”
When news reached him in the middle of January of the ceasefire agreement, he cried, he says over the phone several weeks later. "I see the reports from my colleagues. We reported on the massacre together, we starved and froze. And now, I am so far away. That is difficult. My relatives are spread out across the Gaza Strip. I can’t reach them, just as I cannot reach the mass graves holding my loved ones.”
Does Wael al-Dahdouh plan on returning one day? "Of course. Gaza is a part of me,” he says. "But first, my family and I must return to health.”
